item.title: Zelenskyy says a new European security framework floated by US could benefit Putin
item.description:
Zelenskyy says a new European security framework floated by US could benefit Putin
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says the U.S. has raised the idea of a new postwar security framework for EuropeByHANNA ARHIROVA Associated PressNovember 14, 2026, 6:21 AM
Share
KYIV, Ukraine -- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the United States had raised the possibility of a new security framework for Europe as part of efforts to end Russia’s war in Ukraine, warning that Moscow could use such discussions to weaken NATO and reshape the continent’s borders.
Separately, Ukrainian forces struck a major Russian oil facility supporting Moscow’s war effort, Ukraine's General Staff said in a statement Saturday. Russian
“In my view, this can be dangerous,” Zelenskyy told reporters Friday, referring to the new security framework. “This should not be the main agenda.” His comments were embargoed until Saturday.
He said he believed Moscow was interested in reopening broader questions about European security rather than focusing exclusively on ending the 4 1/2-year war.
“(Russian President Vladimir) Putin’s desire to change borders in Europe is a fact. I am sure this is part of his concept of revising security guarantees in Europe,” he said. “This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations.”
European leaders have stressed that decisions about the continent’s security must be made by Europeans themselves, warning against allowing Russia to dictate the terms of a new security order or negotiate NATO's future.
Zelenskyy said the U.S. had asked for the first time whether Ukraine would withdraw from parts of the Donbas region in eastern Ukraine that Russia does not control if Kyiv were admitted to NATO. He reiterated that Kyiv would not surrender its territory.
Ukraine is discussing a comprehensive security package with its partners that could include specific guarantees from NATO and the European Unio...

item.title: South Sudan postpones first national elections again, to February 2027
item.description:
South Sudan postpones first national elections again, to February 2027
South Sudan has again postponed its first national elections since independence in 2011, moving polling from December to FebruaryByFLORENCE MIETTAUX Associated PressNovember 14, 2026, 5:57 AM
JUBA, South Sudan -- South Sudan has again postponed its first national elections since independence in 2011, moving polling from December to February amid concerns about insecurity, funding shortages and the country’s readiness to vote.
A revised timetable published Saturday by the National Election Commission sets Feb. 11, 2027, as polling day, replacing Dec. 22. The document did not give a reason for the postponement.
The polls have been repeatedly delayed, including in 2022 and 2024. The latest announcement follows warnings that elections could further unravel the country’s fragile peace.
The commission published the timetable on social media on the day voter registration was scheduled to begin. It also sets dates for candidate nominations and campaigning.
A day earlier, commission chairperson Gabriel Bol Deng told journalists in Juba that registration would run from Nov. 14 to Nov. 28 at 3,161 registration centers across the country’s 10 states and three administrative areas.
Deng urged eligible citizens to register and called on political parties, civil society groups, community leaders and the media to help raise public awareness.
South Sudan became independent from Sudan in 2011 after decades of civil war. A new conflict broke out in 2013 between forces loyal to President Salva Kiir and followers of his rival, Riek Machar. A peace deal was signed in 2018 and a transitional government of national unity was formed in 2020.

item.title: Pope's visit to hub of Afro-Peruvian community casts spotlight on African slave trade to Peru
item.description:
Pope's visit to hub of Afro-Peruvian community casts spotlight on African slave trade to Peru
Pope Leo XIV is putting the spotlight on Afro-Peruvians during a visit to a hub of their communityByLUIS ANDRES HENAO Associated Press and NICOLE WINFIELD Associated PressNovember 14, 2026, 2:10 AM
ZAÑA, Peru -- When Susana Baca, the Latin Grammy-winning Afro-Peruvian singer, serenaded Pope Leo XIV upon his arrival in Peru, it was a sign that the visit would provide an unparalleled spotlight on the culture that grew out of the African slave trade in this country.
Baca was also Peru’s first Black Cabinet minister, and she became a leading figure in the campaign to end the discrimination that has long made second-class citizens of Black Peruvians and Peru’s Indigenous peoples.
The U.S.-born Leo, whose own family tree includes enslaved people and slave owners, is expected to highlight Peru’s African-descended community when he visits the hub of Afro-Peruvian culture on Saturday in the city of Zaña.
Leo will lead a prayer meeting at the sanctuary of St. Turibius of Mogrovejo in Zaña, where he often visited to pray while he was bishop of nearby Chiclayo.
In the 16th century, Mogrovejo was the first archbishop of Lima. He defended the rights of Indigenous and enslaved people and was known for having confirmed St. Martin de Porres, the first Black saint of the Americas and the patron saint of racial harmony, social justice and people of multiracial backgrounds.
In his first encyclical, “Magnificent Humanity,” Leo made a sweeping apology for the role of past popes in legitimizing slavery and failing to condemn it for centuries. It was a reference to the series of 15th-century directives from the Vatican that authorized European sovereigns to conquer Africa and the Americas and enslave non-Christians.

item.title: Southeast Asian leaders will call for peaceful resolutions of conflicts. Trump will join final talks
item.description:
Southeast Asian leaders will call for peaceful resolutions of conflicts. Trump will join final talks
Southeast Asian leaders will gather in the Philippine capital this weekend for the annual ASEAN summit that will focus on global conflictsByJIM GOMEZ Associated PressNovember 14, 2026, 1:11 AM
Share
MANILA, Philippines -- Some of the world’s most intractable conflicts will be high on the agenda when Southeast Asian leaders gather in the Philippine capital for annual summit meetings this weekend. U.S. President Donald Trump is expected to join them for the final talks.
The three-day summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and their Asian and Western counterparts starts Sunday in a heavily guarded convention center in Manila Bay.
According to drafts of prepared post-summit communiques seen by The Associated Press, no breakthroughs are expected in the discussions that will focus on calling for the peaceful resolution of the South China Sea disputes, the civil strife in Myanmar and the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine.
This year, the Philippines holds the rotating leadership of ASEAN, a conservative regional bloc of 11 democratic and authoritarian states, including police states. The bloc has managed to keep together such a diverse grouping since its founding in 1967 largely because of its bedrock policy of non-interference in the members' domestic affairs.
In Manila, key rivals will again be face-to-face but no shake-ups are anticipated. ASEAN is known more for its photo-ops that project unity, cultural pomp and pageantry than for effectively dealing with the region's conflicts, including the civil war in Myanmar.
Trump will land in Manila with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday afternoon, after the main ASEAN summit meetings have concluded and the Philippines has turned over the regional bloc’s annual leadership to Singapore.

item.title: Judo star Teddy Riner is taking on what may be his toughest battle in the French presidential race
item.description:
Judo star Teddy Riner is taking on what may be his toughest battle in the French presidential race
Judo star Teddy Riner is taking on what may be his toughest battle in the French presidential raceByJOHN LEICESTER Associated PressNovember 14, 2026, 12:43 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
PARIS -- In a contest of who has the firmer handshake, it's not a stretch to suggest, as he does, that French judo great Teddy Riner would get the better of Donald Trump if ever they were to meet as presidents of their respective countries.
But that's a big “if.”
Even with five Olympic gold medals under his black belt and more than 3.3 million followers on his socials, Riner's newly announced bid for the presidency of France is likely to be a harder contest than many of the judokas he crushed.
The list of celebrities who successfully campaigned for elected office is shorter in France than in the United States, where Trump, Ronald Reagan, Arnold Schwarzenegger, Jesse Ventura, two-time NBA champion Bill Bradley, former Buffalo Bills quarterback Jack Kemp and others turned small-screen, big-screen and sporting stardom into political power.
Two-time Olympic champions David Douillet, in judo, and Jean-François Lamour, in fencing, and Guy Drut, the 110-meter hurdles champion at the Montreal Olympics in 1976, won seats in France's parliament in retirement and served as sports ministers. But Riner is aiming to be the first celebrity to hold France's top office since World War II hero Gen. Charles de Gaulle.
To appear on the ballot for the first round of voting in April, Riner needs a minimum of 500 elected officials to sponsor his candidacy, a requirement designed to not be easy.
The measure, intended to limit the size of the field and filter out fanciful candidacies, is an indication of how France has traditionally regarded running the country as a serious business. It has been in place since the 1981 election and was one of the barriers that foiled a pre...

item.title: French-speaking nations hold a summit in Cambodia but an African conflict threatens a rift
item.description:
French-speaking nations hold a summit in Cambodia but an African conflict threatens a rift
France's President Emmanuel Macron and other leaders are attending a biennial meeting of French-speaking countries and territories in CambodiaByGRANT PECK Associated Press and LORIAN BELANGER Associated PressNovember 13, 2026, 11:57 PM
Share
PHNOM PENH, Cambodia -- PHNOM PENH, Cambodia (AP) — Emmanuel Macron is set to attend a biennial meeting of French-speaking territories beginning Saturday in Cambodia, where the French president contending with public unrest at home will face international political challenges as an African conflict hangs over the proceedings.
The Organisation internationale de la Francophonie is holding the three-day meeting through Monday in the Cambodian capital Phnom Penh. Macron is expected to engage in bilateral discussions and join the summit meeting of the loose confederation of 90 member states and governments comprising 53 full members, five associate members and 32 observers where French is spoken.
Cambodia will take over the summit's chairmanship from Macron, who served as chair in 2024 when France was the host nation.
Before departing for Malaysia on Monday, Macron is scheduled to visit the Angkor World Heritage Site near the city of Siem Reap, where he and King Norodom Sihamoni will mark the completion of a French-supported restoration of the West Mebon temple.
The French leader's trip comes at a time of widespread domestic protests. France’s Interior Ministry said more than 600,000 people took to the streets earlier this month in a demonstration to demand higher wages and support the country’s student protest movement, which has resulted in thousands of arrests, hundreds of injuries and schools set on fire.

item.title: Violent attacks on critics of China in Taiwan raise concern over transnational repression
item.description:
Violent attacks on critics of China in Taiwan raise concern over transnational repression
Comedian Huang Yi-hao was involved in a car accident in September, but it turned out to be a deliberate attackByJOHNSON LAI Associated Press, HUIZHONG WU Associated Press, and KANIS LEUNG Associated PressNovember 13, 2026, 10:00 PM
TAIPEI, Taiwan -- In September, comedian Huang Yi-hao was involved in a car accident, something that could happen to anyone. But one thing stood out: the men in the other car were unusually polite, and even offered to cover his medical bills and the damage to his car.
Huang later received a call from Taiwanese police telling him it wasn't an ordinary accident.
Taipei prosecutors in October charged five men for deliberately attempting to injure Huang in a case that has drawn attention across Taiwan. Authorities say it is part of a growing trend where operatives paid by China harass or attack people on the self-ruled island who are seen as critical of the government in Beijing.
“In the beginning, it was verbal harassment, then it morphed to pouring paint and property damage ... to the level of causing a fake car accident," Chiu Shao-Chou, the commissioner of Taiwan's Criminal investigation Bureau, said. "There's a trend of increasing severity, and that's something we have to take seriously.”
Taiwan is a democratic island claimed by Beijing, which hasn't ruled out using force to annex it. Taiwanese authorities have long worried about Chinese infiltration attempts, including spy plots targeting senior military officials and the president's bodyguards, disinformation schemes during elections or the use of cultural exchanges as a way to spread Communist Party ideology.

item.title: Gold smuggled from war zones entered the UAE despite new regulations, report says
item.description:
Gold smuggled from war zones entered the UAE despite new regulations, report says
A new report says that the United Arab Emirates remains a key destination for gold smuggled from conflict zones despite new regulations on the tradeByHEBA FAROUK MAHFOUZ Associated PressNovember 13, 2026, 12:59 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
CAIRO -- The United Arab Emirates remains a key destination for gold smuggled from war zones despite new regulations on the trade imposed by the government after facing international pressure, a new report says.
Many gold refiners and traders in the UAE are not following the rules and enforcement is lax, according to the report by Swissaid, a Switzerland-based aid and development group. The report recommended that the UAE be added to an international watchlist for possible financial wrongdoing.
The Emirates, which refines and processes the precious metal to send to major markets like Switzerland, India and China, was the second-biggest gold exporter in the world after Switzerland in 2024, a year after the new rules took effect. Smuggled gold from Russia, Yemen and Sudan continues to flow into the UAE, the report says.
The UAE introduced the new guidelines to regulate the gold trade, including responsible sourcing and vetting supply chains, after a global anti-money laundering body raised concerns that the UAE was not doing enough to stop criminals and militants from hiding wealth there.
Despite the new rules, the UAE imported at least 591 tons of illicit gold, valued at $74 billion, the report says. Gold smuggled out of conflict zones, Russia or African countries accounted for 42% of the UAE's total imports of the precious metal in 2024, the report says.
Imports of the precious metal mined and smuggled out of Africa made up nearly half the gold coming into the UAE from the continent, the report said. Some of that gold entered the UAE officially, through third countries. That trade showed a slight increase in 2024, according to the...

item.title: International Criminal Court limits Afghanistan investigation to Taliban crimes
item.description:
International Criminal Court limits Afghanistan investigation to Taliban crimes
Judges at the International Criminal Court have ended the part of the global tribunal’s investigation into Afghanistan that could have involved U.S. military personnelByMOLLY QUELL Associated PressNovember 13, 2026, 12:36 PM
Share
THE HAGUE, Netherlands -- Judges at the International Criminal Court have ended the part of the global tribunal’s investigation into Afghanistan that could have involved U.S. military personnel, instead limiting the probe to crimes committed by the Taliban, according to court filings released Friday.
The ruling comes as the court and 13 current and former staff members are under sanctions by the Trump administration, which is opposed to any investigation into American citizens or U.S. allies, such as Israel.
The decision, which was issued Thursday but only made public on Friday, cites “significant limitations to the Prosecution’s ability to conduct its investigations and secure evidence” in the case. It does not elaborate.
The court's prosecutor's office told The Associated Press it has already appealed the decision.
It is not clear if the decision will mitigate Washington's attacks on the court. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has threatened to “dismantle the ICC — brick by brick, if necessary." The United States is not a member of the court and does not recognize its jurisdiction.

item.title: Hundreds of roaming cows wreak havoc in North Macedonian town, frustrating farmers
item.description:
Hundreds of roaming cows wreak havoc in North Macedonian town, frustrating farmers
Residents of Kriva Palanka in North Macedonia are dealing with a herd of over 1,000 roaming cattleByKONSTANTIN TESTORIDES Associated PressNovember 13, 2026, 11:17 AM
Share
KRIVA PALANKA, North Macedonia -- They descend from the surrounding hills, mostly at night, chomping their way through gardens and crops to satiate their hunger.
For years, residents of Kriva Palanka, a farming town of about 19,000 people in northeastern North Macedonia, have struggled with a herd of roaming cattle that has grown to more than 1,000 animals, destroying property and threatening their livelihood.
It's not just crops. The wandering cows pose a serious risk to the town's water supply and to drivers on a road that leads to neighboring Bulgaria, residents say.
Many fault the country's bureaucratic maze for failing to enforce a 2024 Food and Veterinary Agency order to seize the herd from their three owners.
And even when authorities took legal action against one of the owners, bureaucratic failures derailed the case and allowed the owner to walk free, Kriva Palanka Mayor Sashko Mitovski said.
Mitovski said residents have had enough and are staging protests to urge authorities to take action.
He is asking the conservative government of Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski to declare a 30-day state of emergency in the municipality for authorities to resolve the bovine problem once and for all.
“The number of cattle has increased from 400 four years ago to more than 1,000 today,” Mitovski told The Associated Press.
“We convened a crisis management headquarters because we concluded that, for years, none of the responsible institutions had shown either the willingness, commitment or capacity and resources to resolve the problem.”
Pensioner Lazo Stamenkovski, 71, who lives on the town's outskirts, said the cattle have destroyed more than 150 trees in his orchard.
